summary: To lay the dead in the ground or a tomb, and the grave or tomb they are laid in. Scripture uses it of the patriarchs buried in the one piece of the land of promise Abraham owned (Gen 23), of kings who “lay down with their fathers and were buried”, and of the disgrace of a body left unburied (Jer 16:4; Psa 79:3). The grave is the place of the dead, where Yahweh's faithfulness is not recounted (Psa 88:12), and the place he promises to open: “I will open your graves and bring you up from your graves, my people, and bring you into the land of Israel” (Ezk 37:12), which Jesus echoes, “all who are in the graves will hear his voice and come out” (Jhn 5:28–29). Arabic qabara, Akkadian qebēru, Ugaritic, Phoenician, Ge'ez and Aramaic all have the root with the same meaning.

words.summary: About 130 times. The qal is the act of burying the dead, done by family, friends or the people (Gen 23:4; 50:13; 2Sa 2:4–5); the niphal closes the record of a life, “he died and was buried” and, of the kings, “he lay down with his fathers and was buried”; the piel, a handful of times, is burying in numbers (Num 33:4; Ezk 39:14–15); the pual once (Gen 25:10).

senses.definition: To lay a dead body in a grave or tomb, in the ground or a cave; a duty owed by kin and people to the dead, and owed even to a man hanged for his sin, the same day.

evidence.note: “Give me property for a grave (קֶבֶר) among you, that I may bury (וְאֶקְבְּרָה) my dead from before me.”
Abraham buried Sarah in the cave of the field of Machpelah, in the land of Canaan.
“There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife, there they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife, and there I buried Leah.”
Jacob's sons carried him to Canaan and buried him in the cave of Machpelah.
The bones of Joseph, brought up from Egypt, were buried at Shechem.
The body of a hanged man shall not remain on the tree overnight: “you shall surely bury him (קָבוֹר תִּקְבְּרֶנּוּ) that day, for a hanged man is a curse of God.”
Of Moses: “and he buried him in the valley in the land of Moab … and no man knows his grave to this day”; the subject is Yahweh, of verse 5.
David blesses the men of Jabesh-gilead for the kindness of burying Saul.
“When I die, bury me in the grave in which the man of God is buried; lay my bones beside his bones.”
Men burying a man threw him into Elisha's grave, and when he touched Elisha's bones he lived.
“They have poured out their blood like water round about Jerusalem, and there is none to bury (קוֹבֵר)”: to lie unburied is the mark of judgement.
“They will bury in Topheth until there is no room.”
After the invasion from the north, the house of Israel buries Gog's host for seven months, to cleanse the land.
Joash was buried in the city of David, “but they did not bury him in the graves of the kings”.

senses.definition: To be laid in the grave: the last word on a life, often with “he died” or “he lay down with his fathers”; to be denied it is a judgement.

evidence.note: To Abram: “You will go to your fathers in peace; you will be buried (תִּקָּבֵר) at a good old age.”

The bones of the kings and people brought out of their graves “shall not be gathered or buried”.

senses.definition: To bury the dead in numbers, after a plague or a battle.

evidence.note: The Egyptians “were burying (מְקַבְּרִים)” all their firstborn whom Yahweh had struck.
Joab went up to bury the slain of Edom.
Men set apart to pass through the land burying those left on the face of it, to cleanse it.

“Egypt will gather them, Memphis will bury them.”

words.summary: Nearly seventy times, plural קְבָרִים and קְבָרוֹת. A grave or tomb, owned and handed down in a family (“the grave of his father”), cut in rock or a cave, and so the place of the dead; it can be opened, and Yahweh promises to open Israel's graves and bring them up.

senses.definition: The place a dead body is laid: a family's grave or a cave held as property, a tomb cut in the rock, the graves of the kings.

evidence.note: “Give me property for a grave (אֲחֻזַּת־קֶבֶר) among you.”
The field and the cave “were made sure to Abraham as property for a grave by the sons of Heth”.
Ahithophel “was buried in the grave of his father”.
He laid the man of God's body in his own grave and they lamented over him.
Shebna “has cut out for himself here a grave, carving his grave on the height, a dwelling for himself in the rock”.
Whoever touches a bone of a man or a grave is unclean seven days.
Josiah took the bones out of the graves and burned them on the altar.
“The city, the place of my fathers' graves, lies waste.”
“They did not bury him in the graves of the kings.”
“Is it because there were no graves in Egypt that you have taken us away to die in the wilderness?”

senses.definition: The grave as where the dead lie, cut off and silent, beside the pit and Abaddon; and the place Yahweh promises to open, to bring his people up and into their land.

evidence.note: “Like the slain lying in the grave, whom you remember no more, and they are cut off from your hand.”
“Will your faithfulness be recounted in the grave, your truth in Abaddon?”
“I would have been as though I had not been, carried from the womb to the grave.”
Those who long for death “rejoice exceedingly when they find the grave”.
“My days are extinct, graves are ready for me.”
“They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death”: the servant's burial, fulfilled in Joseph of Arimathea's tomb (Mat 27:57–60).
“Behold, I will open your graves and bring you up from your graves, my people, and bring you into the land of Israel.”
“And you will know that I am Yahweh when I open your graves.”
Assyria's “graves are set in the recesses of the pit (בּוֹר)”.
“You shall be gathered to your graves in peace.”
“All who are in the graves will hear his voice and come out”; the Peshitta has קַבְרֵא, the Hebrew word's Syriac form.

senses.definition: A figure of what swallows up or brings death: an open throat, a quiver, a womb that would have been the grave.

evidence.note: “Their throat is an open grave (קֶבֶר־פָּתוּחַ), they flatter with their tongue.”
Paul quotes Psa 5:10 of all under sin; the Peshitta has קַבְרָא.
“Their quiver is like an open grave.”
“Because he did not kill me from the womb, so that my mother would have been my grave.”

evidence.note: “Their throat is an open grave (τάφος ἀνεῳγμένος)”, quoting Psa 5:10.
“Whitewashed graves (τάφοις), which outwardly appear beautiful but inside are full of dead men's bones.”
The women sat opposite the tomb (τάφου).

evidence.note: “All who are in the tombs (μνημείοις) will hear his voice”: as Ezk 37:12.
“The tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised.”
Lazarus's tomb: “it was a cave, and a stone lay upon it”, as the cave graves of Gen 23.
“They took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb.”

parallels.note: “Abaddon”, destruction, the place of the dead.
“The pit”: the graves of the nations in its recesses.
“The grave”: Heman's life draws near to שְׁאוֹל, and he is like the slain who lie in the קֶבֶר.

opposites.note: “Womb”: the two ends of a life, from the womb to the grave.

words.summary: Fourteen times, also spelled קְבוּרָה: a grave, like קֶבֶר, and the burial itself, the act or the honour of being buried.

senses.definition: A person's grave, marked or known, or a family's tomb.

evidence.note: “Jacob set up a pillar over her grave; that is the pillar of Rachel's grave to this day.”
“Carry me out of Egypt and bury me in their grave.”
“No man knows his grave (קְבֻרָתוֹ) to this day.”
“By Rachel's tomb in the border of Benjamin.”
They buried Ahaziah “in his grave with his fathers in the city of David”.
Assyria's company “round about her grave”.

senses.definition: Being buried, the burial due to a man; to lack it, or have a beast's, is disgrace.

evidence.note: “With the burial of a donkey (קְבוּרַת חֲמוֹר) he will be buried, dragged and thrown out.”
Babylon's king “will not be joined with them in burial”, cast out of his grave (v. 19).
A man with a hundred children and long life, if “he has no burial”, a stillborn is better than he.
With the price of blood the chief priests bought the potter's field “as a burial place (εἰς ταφήν) for strangers”.

words.summary: The station in the wilderness where the people who craved meat were struck and buried (Num 11:31–34): the plural of קֶבֶר with תַּאֲוָה “craving, desire”, and scripture gives the reason for the name. A place, so it has no name entry.

senses.definition: The camp between Sinai and Hazeroth named for the graves of those who craved.

evidence.note: “He called the name of that place Kibroth-hattaavah, because there they buried the people who craved.”
From there to Hazeroth.
In the list of stations.
“At Taberah and at Massah and at Kibroth-hattaavah you provoked Yahweh.”
“That we should not crave evil things as they also craved”: the lesson of the place.

words.summary: The Peshitta's ܩܒܪ (qbar), for θάπτω and συνθάπτω, in the burial of the dead and of Jesus, and of baptism as burial with him. Its pael “heap up” (Rom 12:20) has no clear link to the root's sense.

evidence.note: “Let me first go and bury (אֶקְבּוּר) my father.”
John's disciples took up his body and buried it.
Bound in linen with spices, “as is the custom of the Jews to bury”.
The young men carried out Ananias and buried him.
Devout men buried Stephen.

senses.definition: Be buried; of baptism, be buried with Christ.

evidence.note: David “died and was buried (אֶתְקְבַר), and his tomb (קְבוּרֵהּ) is with us”.
“That he was buried, and rose on the third day.”
“The rich man also died and was buried.”
“We were buried with him by baptism into death, that as Christ was raised from the dead … we also should walk in newness of life.”
“Buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him.”

senses.definition: Once, heap coals of fire on an enemy's head, quoting Pro 25:22, where the Hebrew verb is חָתָה. How it comes from “bury” is not clear.

evidence.note: “In doing this you will heap (תְּקַבַּר) coals of fire on his head.”
The verse quoted.

senses.definition: A grave or rock tomb; Jesus' tomb; the graves the dead will come out of.

Quoting Psa 5:10, “their throat is an open grave”.

The women came to see the tomb.
Mary stood at the tomb weeping.

“You build the tombs of the prophets.”

words.summary: The Peshitta's ܩܒܘܪܐ (qbūrā), its commonest word for Jesus' tomb, for μνημεῖον.

senses.definition: A tomb; the tombs among which the possessed man lived; Jesus' new tomb.

“The tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who slept arose.”
He had his dwelling among the tombs.

doctrine.statement: The grave is where the dead lie: Heman counts himself “like the slain lying in the grave, whom you remember no more”, and asks, “Will your faithfulness be recounted in the grave, your truth in Abaddon? … Do the dead rise and praise you?” (Psa 88:6, 11–12). Job would have been “as though I had not been, carried from the womb to the grave” (Job 10:19), and the Preacher says “the dead know nothing … there is no work or thought or knowledge or wisdom in the grave (שְׁאוֹל)” (Ecc 9:5, 10). Even David, the man after God's heart, “died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day … for David did not ascend into the heavens” (Act 2:29, 34). From the verses: the dead are in the grave, not elsewhere; they do not remember or praise; their hope is not in the grave but in being brought out of it.

Yahweh says to Israel, “Behold, I will open your graves and bring you up from your graves, my people, and bring you into the land of Israel; and you will know that I am Yahweh when I open your graves” (Ezk 37:12–13). Daniel is told “many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake” (Dan 12:2), and Jesus says “the hour is coming in which all who are in the graves will hear his voice and come out, those who did good to a resurrection of life” (Jhn 5:28–29). Scripture gives the pattern beforehand: a dead man touched Elisha's bones in the grave and lived (2Ki 13:21); at Jesus' death “the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised, and came out of the tombs after his resurrection” (Mat 27:52–53); and the gospel is “that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day” (1Co 15:3–4). From the verses: the dead come back to life by coming out of the grave at Christ's voice, bodily, as he did; resurrection is out of the grave, not out of the body.

Yahweh promised Abraham, “all the land that you see, to you I will give it, and to your seed for ever” (Gen 13:15; 17:8), yet the only part of it Abraham ever held was a grave he bought: “give me property for a grave among you, that I may bury my dead” (Gen 23:4, 20). There Sarah, Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah and Leah were buried, Jacob asked to be carried back to it, and Joseph's bones were brought up from Egypt to the land (Gen 25:9–10; 49:29–31; 50:13, 24–25; Jos 24:32). Stephen says Yahweh “gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's length, yet promised to give it to him for a possession, and to his seed after him”, and that the fathers were laid “in the tomb that Abraham bought” (Act 7:5, 16); “these all died in faith, not having received the promises” (Heb 11:13, 39–40). From the verses: the promise to Abraham himself was not kept in his lifetime; the burials in the land were faith that it will be, and Ezk 37:12 joins the opening of the graves to bringing the dead “into the land of Israel”.

The law said of a man hanged on a tree, “his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall surely bury him that day, for a hanged man is a curse of God” (Deu 21:23); the Jews asked that the bodies be taken down before the sabbath (Jhn 19:31), and Paul says “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us” (Gal 3:13). Isaiah's servant was given “his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death” (Isa 53:9), and the rich man Joseph of Arimathea laid him in his own new tomb hewn in the rock (Mat 27:57–60). His burial is part of the gospel, between his death and his raising (1Co 15:3–4), and baptism is being “buried with him into death, that as Christ was raised from the dead … we also should walk in newness of life” (Rom 6:4; Col 2:12). From the verses: he truly died and was laid in the grave as the law and the prophet foretold, and the believer is joined to his death, burial and raising in baptism.

note: Drafted 2026-11-18. Root key קבר; all four BDB keys assigned: s.ah.aa verb, s.ah.ab קֶבֶר, s.ah.ad קְבֻרָה, s.ah.ac the place קִבְרוֹת הַתַּאֲוָה (kept as a word, pos name, like other places; TIPNR has it only as a place, Kibroth-hattaavah@Num.11.34, so no name entry). No personal name is formed from the root. No letter of the root is a merged letter, so no `sounds`. Peshitta words from SEDRA root 1617 XBR (lexemes 2733–2737) with verses from the BFBS word list; SEDRA lists the ethpeel tokens under the verb lexeme (Act 2:29, Luk 16:22, Rom 6:4, Col 2:12, 1Co 15:4). The pael “heap up” (Rom 12:20, Pro 25:22's חָתָה) has no evident link to “bury”; check Payne Smith and Brockelmann for whether it is a separate root. Not checked by page: dulat-2015 (Ugaritic qbr), krahmalkov-2000 (Phoenician QBR; KAI 14, Eshmunazar, is a lead for the grave/bury curse), leslau-1987 (qabara); add page numbers. Sabaic qbr “tomb” (Biella, SabaWeb) and Nabataean/Palmyrene qbrʾ “tomb” are leads not followed. Deu 34:6 MT וַיִּקְבֹּר “he buried”, subject Yahweh from v. 5; the Septuagint has ἔθαψαν “they buried”. Ezk 39:11–16, the burial of Gog's host, read with Ezk 38–39 as the northern invasion. Jastrow's Mishnaic sense “womb” for קֶבֶר is later Hebrew; Jer 20:17 is the only biblical contact and is kept as a figure.
